Couple of things wrong with your premise. ATMs didn't disproportionately displace tellers which is true, what it did was to allow them to do other tasks that they were either already required to do or take on new activities and tasks that they weren't doing before because someone else was doing those tasks. So the ATM machine increased efficiencies directly for the teller, but further down up the chain, people were displaced and lost their jobs because the teller could now do more. In this example, there was a solution that had a limited purpose and that solution (the ATM) machine could only do one thing...hand out money so that tellers could do less of that ONE THING. AI on the other hand, as it scales, is constantly growing and becoming more and more and more complex and capable of doing the tasks further up the human resource chain. So as with the ATMs and tellers where only 1 or possibly 2 upstream levels of human labor resources were displaced, AI will continue to move further and further up the chain as it grows and scales. Eventually, any what I call virtual labor (work that is done electronically,/digitally) by a human behind a computer (which is a vast majority of work in the American labor market today) will be displaced via AI and automation. The ONLY labor that won't be displaced in the near term (~20 years) is physical labor where a person has to know a specific trade/skill and requires hands-on interaction to the work (think: plumber, electrician/mechanic/etc...). Even those jobs will be replaced once AI and automation merge with humanoid style robotics with the dexterity capabilities of human beings today. This is already in motion and will be here in our lifetimes. So this cope that jobs won't be replaced by AI is just flat out wrong. The first phase is efficiency improvements for sure and I agree with that. But eventually, human beings will be displaced in 90%+ of the labor market. Just a matter of time.
